questions.question_text: The diagnosis of induced delusional disorder is most commonly found in which of the following groups?

options.text: Groups of men rather than women
Groups of women rather than men

questions.explanation:
Most cases of induced delusional disorder occur within the nuclear family, usually between married or common-law couples (52%) or sisters (24%).
Ref: Cipriani G et al. A contagious disorder: Folie à deux and dementia. American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease & Other Dementias®. 2018 Nov;33(7):415-22.

questions.question_text: The multi-axial version of ICD, prior to ICD-11, consisted of how many axes?
questions.explanation: The multi-axial version of ICD-10 used three axes: Axis 1 - the mental disorder (also personality disorder and mental handicap); Axis 2 - the degree of disability; and Axis 3 - current psychosocial problems.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following of those historical subtypes was associated with the worst prognosis?
questions.explanation: The onset of hebephrenic schizophrenia is insidious, usually in the early second decade. The course is often progressively downhill. There is a rapid development of negative symptoms and disorganised behaviour. Severe deterioration without remission occurs over time. A recovery from the first episode was said to be rare in typical cases of the hebephrenic syndrome. But the validity of these subtypes were increasingly questioned, leading to their drop from modern classifications such as DSM-5 and ICD-11.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a correct statement regarding anorexia?

options.text: Anorexic women are more likely to have a history of childhood sexual abuse compared to depressed women
A significant heritability exists for bulimia but not anorexia
The concordance rate for monozygotic twins is higher than dizygotic twins
Persistent preoccupation with eating is a characteristic feature
Social class distribution of prevalence of anorexia is even

correct_answer.text: The concordance rate for monozygotic twins is higher than dizygotic twins

correct_answers.text: The concordance rate for monozygotic twins is higher than dizygotic twins

questions.explanation:
Concordance of monozygotic:dizygotic = 65%:32%. There is no excess of childhood physical or sexual abuse in anorexia nervosa compared to psychiatric controls. Patients with anorexia nervosa have body image distortion (dread of fatness, overvalued ideas, imposed low weight threshold).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 411.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning cyclothymia?

options.text: It is commonly associated with endocrine disturbances
The diagnosis can be made if there is a past history of bipolar disorder
Mood stabilisers are of no use in management
Hypomania is the most common reason for seeking help
It often fails to come to medical attention

correct_answer.text: It often fails to come to medical attention

correct_answers.text: It often fails to come to medical attention

questions.explanation:
Because cyclothymic mood swings are relatively mild and periods of mood elevation may be enjoyable (with increased activity and productivity, self-confidence, and sociability), cyclothymia frequently fails to come to medical attention. The person may often present either because of the impact of the depressive episodes on social and work situations or because of problems related to comorbid drug or alcohol misuse. If pharmacological treatment is contemplated, this usually consists of a trial of a mood stabiliser.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 348-349.

questions.question_text: Which of the following delusions is least likely to be associated with a delusional disorder?
questions.explanation:
Delusional disorder is an uncommon condition in which patients present with circumscribed symptoms of non-bizarre delusions (DSM-5 allows ‘with bizarre content’; ICD-11 does not specify), but with absence of prominent hallucinations and no thought disorder, mood disorder, or significant flattening of affect. DSM-5 subtypes include erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory, and somatic. ICD-11 states that delusions typically persist for at least 3 months and often much longer.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 230.

questions.question_text: Ganser syndrome is included in ICD-11 under which of the following chapters?

options.text: Disorders of bodily distress or bodily experience

questions.explanation:
Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal activities of daily living, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 236.
Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1-22.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered a core symptom of schizophrenia in ICD-11?
questions.explanation:
Although first-rank symptoms have been somewhat deemphasised in ICD-11, a diagnosis of schizophrenia requires the presence of at least two of seven symptom categories, including at least one of four ‘core’ symptoms. Core symptoms are delusions; hallucinations; experiences of influence, passivity, or control; and disorganised thinking (formal thought disorder). ‘Negative symptoms’ (such as affective flattening, alogia or paucity of speech, avolition, asociality, and anhedonia) represent one of the seven symptom categories, but not a core category in ICD-11.
Ref: Stein DJ et al. Mental, behavioral and neurodevelopmental disorders in the ICD-11: an international perspective on key changes and controversies. BMC medicine. 2020 Dec;18(1):1-24.
International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Mood incongruity (such as inappropriate laughter, smiling, “buffoonery”, or weeping) has been considered an important sign in schizophrenia, though it is not specifically included in current diagnostic systems. It was added in DSM-III and dropped in DSM-IV. ‘Mood-congruent’ describes a secondary symptom which is understandable in light of an abnormal mood state (e.g a severely depressed patient developing a delusion that they are in severe debt, or a manic patient developing a delusion that they are exceptionally wealthy).
Ref: Kendler KS. Phenomenology of schizophrenia and the representativeness of modern diagnostic criteria. JAMA psychiatry. 2016 Oct 1;73(10):1082-92.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 114.

questions.question_text: The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Hypochondriasis is the preoccupation with the fear of having a serious disease, which persists despite negative medical investigations and appropriate reassurance, with subsequent distress and impaired function.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 870.

questions.question_text: What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Hypochondriasis is an anxiety state. A patient with hypochondriasis may hold a belief as an overvalued idea bordering on delusional intensity. The patient in question here seems to hold the belief with absolute conviction; ICD-11 allows a specifier "with poor insight" for an individual who, either most or all of the time, is "convinced that the disorder-specific beliefs are true and they cannot accept an alternative explanation for their experience. The lack of insight exhibited by the individual does not vary markedly as a function of anxiety level".
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 870.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of narcolepsy?
questions.explanation:
Classic symptoms of narcolepsy include: excessive daytime sleepiness; cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone during wakefulness that is evoked by strong, mainly positive, emotions); sleep paralysis (sometimes up to 10 minutes long); and hypnagogic hallucinations (vivid hallucinations on falling asleep) or hypnopompic hallucinations (hallucinations when the individual is waking up).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 450.
Kornum BR et al. Narcolepsy. Nature reviews Disease primers. 2017 Feb 9;3(1):1-9.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a common clinical feature of mania?

options.text: Elevated mood out of keeping with the circumstances

questions.explanation:
Clinical features of mania:
- Elevated mood (out of keeping with circumstances)
- Increased energy which may manifest as overactivity and/or reduced need for sleep
- Formal thought disorder which may manifest as pressured speech, flight of ideas, and/or racing thoughts
- Increased self-esteem, evident as over-optimistic ideation, grandiosity, reduced social inhibitions, and/or over-familiarity
- Reduced attention and increased distractibility
- Tendency to engage in behaviour that may have serious consequences (e.g. spending recklessly, inappropriate sexual encounters)
- Other behavioural manifestations, including excitement, irritability, aggressiveness, and suspiciousness
- Marked disruption of work, usual social activities, and family life
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 320-321.

questions.question_text: The term schizoaffective psychosis was coined by
questions.explanation:
The term schizoaffective psychosis was introduced by the Russian-born American psychiatrist Jacob Kasanin in 1933. The earlier concepts of schizoaffective disorder regarded this diagnosis as a good prognosis schizophrenia, with psychoanalytic explanations.
Ref: Kasanin JA. The acute schizoaffective psychoses. American Journal of Psychiatry. 1933 Jul;90(1):97-126.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about patients with anorexia nervosa?

options.text: The illness has less mortality rate than schizophrenia
The most common cause for presentation is comorbid personality disorder
The incidence is 35% in the monozygotic twins of affected patients
The incidence is 15% in the dizygotic twins of affected patients
There is no association between social class and development of anorexia

correct_answer.text: There is no association between social class and development of anorexia

correct_answers.text: There is no association between social class and development of anorexia

questions.explanation:
Anorexia nervosa has the highest rate of mortality among all mental disorders. Though anorexia nervosa is found globally, it is considered more prevalent in some Western societies where cultural influences promote thinness as the ideal body shape. However, there is no evidence that differences such as ethnicity or socioeconomic status make it more likely that that a member of any one group will have an eating disorder. The genetic concordance of anorexia nervosa is MZ:DZ = 65%:32%.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 410-411.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. NICE guideline Eating Disorders: recognition and treatment 2017.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not indicative of excessive preoccupation with body weight or shape in anorexia nervosa?

options.text: Repeatedly checking one’s reflection in mirrors
Refusal to have mirrors at home
Avoiding knowing the calorie content of food

correct_answer.text: Avoiding knowing the calorie content of food

correct_answers.text: Avoiding knowing the calorie content of food

questions.explanation:
Anorexia nervosa is characterised by significantly low body weight for the individual’s height, age, and developmental stage that is not due to another health condition or to the unavailability of food. Low body weight or shape is central to the person’s self-evaluation or is inaccurately perceived to be normal or even excessive. Preoccupation with weight or shape, when not explicitly reported, may be manifested by behaviours such as repeatedly checking body weight using scales; repeatedly checking one’s body shape using tape measures or reflection in mirrors; constantly monitoring the calorie content of food or searching for information on how to lose weight; or by extreme avoidant behaviours, such as refusal to have mirrors at home, avoidance of tight-fitting clothes, or refusal to know one’s weight or purchase clothing with specified sizing.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: The progression of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

options.text: Shows initial low symptom levels with an increase in symptoms over time
Evolves into chronic distress with high symptom levels for most people
Fluctuates over time and is not static
Is concretely determined in the acute phase following trauma

correct_answer.text: Fluctuates over time and is not static

correct_answers.text: Fluctuates over time and is not static

questions.explanation:
The understanding that PTSD follows a linear course has been challenged in recent years by evidence that the severity of the disorder fluctuates over time, that it can worsen or remit, and that this pattern can keep recurring, with the result that one’s PTSD status is not static. Studies have demonstrated a resilient class which consistently shows few PTSD symptoms, a recovery class with initial distress followed by gradual remission, a delayed reaction class with initial low symptom levels but increased symptoms over time, and a chronic distress class with consistently high PTSD levels. There is also evidence that the PTSD syndrome develops over time. In the acute phase after trauma, PTSD symptoms appear more loosely interconnected, while they become more closely related with the known factors (e.g., re-experiencing, active avoidance) as time progresses.
Ref: Bryant RA. Post‐traumatic stress disorder: a state‐of‐the‐art review of evidence and challenges. World Psychiatry. 2019 Oct;18(3):259-69.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most likely ICD-11 diagnosis?

options.text: Mental disorder associated with the puerperium, with psychotic symptoms
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

correct_answer.text: Mental disorder associated with the puerperium, with psychotic symptoms

correct_answers.text: Mental disorder associated with the puerperium, with psychotic symptoms

questions.explanation:
This scenario depicts postpartum psychosis. Postpartum psychosis has three common clinical presentations: prominent affective symptoms (mania or depression with psychotic symptoms), schizophreniform disorder, or acute organic psychosis. ICD-11 recommends using this term for significant mental disorders that are commencing within about 6 weeks after delivery that include delusions, hallucinations, or other psychotic symptoms. This designation should not be used for the so-called postpartum blues.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 494-495.

questions.question_text: Most children with selective mutism also meet diagnostic criteria for which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Selective mutism is characterised by the persistent failure to speak in specific settings (e.g. school) where there is an expectation to speak. It begins after normal speech has been acquired, and there is full use of language at home/with family. Patients may remain wholly silent or near-silent, in some cases only whispering in a school setting. In rare cases, a child is mute at home but not in school. Social anxiety is almost always present.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 687.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 201.

questions.question_text: The term schizophrenia was coined by
questions.explanation:
Eugene Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia (1911) , which replaced dementia praecox in the literature. Deriving it from the ancient Greek words ‘schizo’ (‘I split’) and ‘phren’ (‘mind’), he chose the term to express the presence of schisms among thought, emotions, and behaviour in patients with the disorder.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1099.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 182.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding schizophrenia subtypes in ICD-11?

options.text: Catatonia is considered to be a subtype of schizophrenia
Subtypes of schizophrenia include paranoid and hebephrenic
Schizophrenia subtypes have shown predictive validity
All subtypes of schizophrenia have been eliminated

correct_answer.text: All subtypes of schizophrenia have been eliminated

correct_answers.text: All subtypes of schizophrenia have been eliminated

questions.explanation:
A significant change in ICD-11 is the elimination of all subtypes of schizophrenia (e.g., paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic), due to their lack of predictive validity or utility in treatment selection. In lieu of the subtypes, a set of dimensional descriptors has been introduced. In ICD-10, catatonia was included as one of the subtypes of schizophrenia and as one of the organic disorders (i.e., organic catatonic disorder). In recognition of the fact that the syndrome of catatonia can occur in association with a variety of mental disorders, a new diagnostic grouping for catatonia (at the same hierarchical level as mood disorders, anxiety and fear-related disorders, etc.) has been added in ICD-11.
Ref: Reed GM et al. Innovations and changes in the ICD‐11 classification of mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. World Psychiatry. 2019 Feb;18(1):3-19.

questions.question_text: This is guided by which of the following principles of classification?
questions.explanation:
The ideal diagnostic system labels diseases according to aetiology. The aetiology of most mental disorders in unknown, so we tend towards a diagnostic system based on common clinical features, shared natural history, common treatment response, or a combination of all three. Diagnosis leads to the consideration of individual diseases as members of groups contained within a hierarchy – a form of classification system.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 10.

Cannabis use, especially in adolescence, confers a twofold increased risk of later schizophrenia. The highest risk is for younger adolescents (fourfold increased risk for those using cannabis by age 15).
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the treatment and management of psychosis and schizophrenia in adults. Updated edition 2014.
Hollis C. Schizophrenia in children and adolescents. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Sep;21(5):333-41.

questions.explanation:
Psychiatric sequelae of stroke include cognitive disorders and post-stroke depression.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 176.

questions.question_text: Which of the following personality types is classified as a Cluster A personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
DSM-5 uses three broad clusters to organise the categories of personality disorders:
- Cluster A (odd/eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal
- Cluster B (emotional/dramatic): antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic, borderline
- Cluster C (fearful/anxious): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 561.

questions.question_text: He is most likely to have which of the following diagnosable psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation:
Conduct disorder is characterised by a repetitive and persistent pattern of antisocial, aggressive or defiant behaviours that defy age-appropriate societal norms or rules. Depending on the age/stage of the child, this may include: aggression/cruelty to people and/or animals, destruction of property, bullying, deceitfulness, lying/blaming others, theft, fire setting, truancy/running away from home, severe provocative or disobedient/defiant behaviour, forced sexual activity, use of a weapon.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 664.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the most appropriate medication for his condition?
questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines recommend the following for bipolar depression:
If depression is moderate-severe and patient is not taking medication to treat bipolar, offer:
1. Fluoxetine combined with olanzapine (OFC)
2. Quetiapine on its own
3. If patient prefers, either olanzapine or lamotrigine on its own
4. If no response to either of first two options, consider lamotrigine on its own
If depression is moderate-severe and patient is already taking lithium, check lithium level and optimize; if lithium is maximized, add olanzapine+fluoxetine, add quetiapine, add olanzapine, or add lamotrigine
If depression is moderate-severe and patient is already taking valproate, considering inc to max dose within the therapeutic range; if already done, add olanzapine+fluoxetine, add quetiapine, add olanzapine, or add lamotrigine
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the assessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and young people in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020.

questions.question_text: According to ICD-11, acute and transient psychotic disorder is characterised by an acute onset of a clear psychotic state from a non-psychotic state within a period of:
questions.explanation:
Acute and transient psychotic disorder is characterised by acute onset of psychotic symptoms that emerge without a prodrome and reach their maximal severity within two weeks. Symptoms may include delusions, hallucinations, disorganisation of thought processes, perplexity or confusion, and disturbances of affect or mood. Catatonia-like motor disturbances may be present. Symptoms typically change rapidly, both in nature and intensity, from day to day, or even within a single day. The duration of the episode does not exceed 3 months, and most commonly lasts from a few days to 1 month.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of patients with obsessive compulsive personality disorder include reluctance to delegate; perfectionism interfering with completion of tasks; miserly spending and hoarding of money; inability to discard worthless objects; excessive devotion to work and productivity; preoccupation with details, rules, lists, order, schedules; inflexibility about morality and ethics; rigidity and stubbornness.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 566.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not categorised as an autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?
questions.explanation: In DSM-5 the previous categories of Autistic Disorder, Asperger’s Disorder and Pervasive Developmental Disorder-NOS and Childhood Disintegrative Disorder (Hellers syndrome) were replaced by the diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. Additionally, the DSM-5 also reduced social-related elements of autism into social communication impairment and repetitive/restricted behaviours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a poor prognostic factor for schizophrenia in terms of relapse/recovery from the illness?
questions.explanation:
Poor prognostic factors in schizophrenia include: poor premorbid adjustment/functioning; insidious onset; young onset (childhood or adolescence); cognitive impairment; enlarged ventricles; male sex; negative symptoms (not mood symptoms, which are a positive prognostic factor).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 207.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 350.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following can be a discriminating symptom while making a clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Thought withdrawal is a first rank symptom for a diagnosis of schizophrenia. This is considered to be a discriminating symptom while making a clinical diagnosis. First rank symptoms of schizophrenia are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not.
First rank symptoms can be categorised as follows:
- Auditory hallucinations (voices heard arguing, thought echo, running commentary)
- Delusions of thought interference (thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting)
- Delusions of control (passivity of affect, passivity of impulse, passivity of volitions, somatic passivity)
- Delusional perception (a primary delusion of any content that is reported by the patient as having arisen, following the experience of a normal perception)
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 78.

questions.question_text: What percentage of non-schizophrenic patients with psychosis exhibit first rank symptoms of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Kurt Schneider enumerated a number of symptoms which he believed were of first-rank importance in differentiating schizophrenia from related illnesses. According to the International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia, 58% of patients with acute schizophrenia exhibited at least one first rank symptom. Generally, the prevalence of first-rank symptoms in schizophrenia is reported to range between 25 and 88%, and in a Cochrane diagnostic test review it was 57%. However,
at least 20% of people with schizophrenia never exhibit a first rank symptom while almost 10% of non-schizophrenic patients exhibit them. This value can be higher (19%, per Soares-Weiser et al., 2015) in studies that specifically examine FRS.
Ref: Mitchell AJ. First-rank symptoms: a first-rank diagnostic test?. BJPsych Advances. 2015 May;21(3):147-9.
Soares-Weiser , K, Maayan , N, Bergman , H et al ( 2015 ) First rank symptoms for schizophrenia (Review). Cochrane Library , issue 1 (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD010653.pub2/pdf ).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true?

options.text: He has a specific phobia as he has an irrational fear
He has no specific phobia as fear of darkness is common
He has a specific phobia with loss of insight
He has no specific phobia as he does not have an avoidance behaviour
He has a specific phobia as he has it since childhood

correct_answer.text: He has no specific phobia as he does not have an avoidance behaviour

correct_answers.text: He has no specific phobia as he does not have an avoidance behaviour

questions.explanation:
In phobias of all kinds, there is an avoidance of the feared situation. Specific phobias are restricted to specific situations such as proximity to certain animals, natural phenomenon such as heights, thunder, darkness, flying, being trapped in closed spaces, urinating or defecating in public toilets, eating certain foods, dentistry, or the sight of blood or injury.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 69.

questions.question_text: This is suggestive of
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of patients with avoidant personality disorder include avoiding jobs with significant interpersonal contact for fear of criticism or rejection; unwillingness to get involved unless certain of being liked; restraint in relationships because of fear of being ridiculed; preoccupation with being criticized or rejected; social inhibition because of feelings of inadequacy; viewing self as inferior; reluctance to take risks because of possible embarrassment.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 565.

questions.question_text: Which of the following culture-bound syndromes refer to fear of turning into a cannibal?
questions.explanation:
Witiko psychosis (or Windigo) refers to a person developing the delusion of transforming into a cannibalistic monster and craving human flesh under the threat of starvation in severely cold weather. (Note: The term 'witiko' is more appropriate to capture this condition, and the Western interpretation of what is described as Windigo being attributed to the ethnic groups of Cree and Metis people has been disputed.)
Ref: Tseng WS. From peculiar psychiatric disorders through culture-bound syndromes to culture-related specific syndromes. Transcultural psychiatry. 2006 Dec;43(4):554-76.
Carlson ND. Reviving Witiko (Windigo): An ethnohistory of “cannibal monsters” in the Athabasca district of northern Alberta, 1878–1910. Ethnohistory. 2009;56(3):355-94.

questions.question_text: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Symptoms of benzodiazepine withdrawal include anxiety, insomnia, tremor, agitation, headache, nausea, sweating, depersonalisation, seizures, and delirium. Sometimes grand mal seizures can occur. Kinaesthetic hallucinations can occur in schizophrenia or in organic states such as alcohol intoxication and during benzodiazepine withdrawal. Kinaesthetic hallucinations affect the muscles and joints, and the patient feels that their limbs are being twisted, pulled, or moved.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 638.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 34.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, this condition is described in which of the following chapters?

options.text: Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours

correct_answer.text: Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours

correct_answers.text: Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours

questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, ‘Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours’ are mental and behavioural disorders that develop as a result of the use of predominantly psychoactive substances, including medications, or specific repetitive rewarding and reinforcing behaviours. For disorders due to use of opioids, this includes harmful pattern of use of opioids and opioid dependence.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which term refers to 'discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication'?
questions.explanation:
Alcohol-induced amnesia or blackouts or ‘palimpsest’ are not included in DSM-5/ICD-11. This is characterised by discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. Patients will report a gap in their memory lasting for several hours, with global or partial amnesia for their actions during that time. The patient’s behaviour is usually characteristic of their normal behaviour when intoxicated. There is a breakdown in transfer of information from short-term to long-term storage which occurs while immediate (very brief short-term) and remote (long-term; formed prior to intoxication) memory abilities remain intact. Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories, a process that is thought to involve the hippocampus and related temporal lobe structures. Alcohol facilitates faster forgetting. Rapid forgetting is a hallmark of hippocampal dysfunction.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 600.
Hermens DF, Lagopoulos J. Binge drinking and the young brain: A mini review of the neurobiological underpinnings of alcohol-induced blackout. Frontiers in psychology. 2018 Jan 19;9:12.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 277-278.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chapters will his diagnosis fall under in ICD-11?

options.text: Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders

correct_answer.text: Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders

correct_answers.text: Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders

questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, schizoaffective disorder is characterised by schizophrenic and affective symptoms that are simultaneously present for at least 1 month, and both are equally prominent. Schizoaffective disorder is in the ‘schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders’ grouping.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 228.
International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning brain injury and schizophrenia?

options.text: Genetic predisposition to schizophrenia has no influence on vulnerability for psychosis after brain injury
Brain injury increases risk of non-affective psychosis more than affective psychosis
Psychosis related to brain injury is usually acute in onset
Brain injury markedly increases likelihood of developing schizophrenia
Children are more susceptible to schizophrenia following brain injury than adults

correct_answer.text: Brain injury increases risk of non-affective psychosis more than affective psychosis

correct_answers.text: Brain injury increases risk of non-affective psychosis more than affective psychosis

questions.explanation:
A schizophrenia-like psychotic disorder after brain injury occurs relatively rarely 1-5 years after injury and is associated with frontal and temporal damage. Persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations are the more frequent postinjury psychotic sequelae, with low rates of negative symptoms (e.g., anhedonia), diverging from the symptom profile common to schizophrenia. Children have less psychopathology after brain injury than adults due to increased brain plasticity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is believed by some to represent a point on a continuum of 'unitary psychosis' lying quantitatively between schizophrenic and mood symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Schizoaffective disorder has features of both affective disorder and schizophrenia which are present in approximately equal proportion. Its nosological status is uncertain, since some believe it to be a variant of schizophrenia; others, bipolar disorder; and some believe it represents a point on a continuum of ‘unitary psychosis’, lying between schizophrenia and mood disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best test to differentiate delirium from dementia?

questions.question_text: According to ICD 11 what is the minimum duration required for a diagnosis of hypomania?

According to ICD-11, a hypomanic episode is a persistent mood state lasting at least several days characterised by mild elevation of mood or increased irritability and increased activity or a subjective experience of increased energy, accompanied by other characteristic symptoms such as rapid speech, rapid or racing thoughts, increased self-esteem, an increase in sexual drive or sociability, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, or impulsive or reckless behaviour.

questions.question_text: Autism spectrum disorder typically first becomes evident at what age?
questions.explanation:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is typically evident during the second year of life, and in severe cases, a lack of developmentally appropriate interest in social interactions may be noted even in the first year. However, in milder cases, core impairments in ASD may not be identified for several more years. ASD in children with normal intellectual function and mild impairment in language function may not be identified until middle childhood when both academic and social demands increase.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 122.

questions.question_text: The term simple schizophrenia was added to the categories of existing schizophrenias by
questions.explanation:
In 1896, Emil Kraepelin described and separated the two major forms of insanity on the basis of different symptoms, course, and outcome. The first, ‘manic-depressive insanity’, had a relapsing and remitting course, with full recovery after each episode. The second grouped together catatonia, hebephrenia, and the paranoid psychoses under the term ‘dementia praecox’, which had a progressive, deteriorating course. Eugen Bleuler added ‘simple schizophrenia’ to Kraepelin’s subtypes and did not consider hallucinations, delusions, and catatonic symptoms to be necessary for the diagnosis. He believed the disorder to be due to a ‘loosening of associations’ between psychic functions, with fundamental symptoms being thought disorder, blunting/incongruity of affect, autism, and ambivalence.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 182.

Symptoms of mild neurocognitive disorder include cognitive slowing and memory deficits, as well as motor slowing and subtle incoordination. Clinical features of HIV-associated dementia are classified as cognitive (subcortical dementia, focal cognitive deficits, amnesia, mutism), motor (movement disorders e.g. tremor, ataxia, choreo-athetosis, spasticity, myoclonus), and affective (depression, apathy, agitation, disinhibition, mania).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 149.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding delusional disorder according to ICD-11 diagnostic criteria?

questions.explanation:
Delusional disorder is characterised by the development of a delusion or set of related delusions, typically persisting for at least 3 months and often much longer, in the absence of a depressive, manic, or mixed mood episode. The delusions are variable in content across individuals, but typically stable within individuals, although they may evolve over time. Other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (i.e. clear and persistent hallucinations, negative symptoms, disorganised thinking, or experiences of influence, passivity, or control) are not present, although various forms of perceptual disturbances (e.g. hallucinations, illusions, misidentification of persons) thematically related to the delusion are still consistent with the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding PTSD is true?

options.text: Specific EEG changes occur in chronic PTSD

PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the trauma
Autonomic hyperarousal symptoms are usually rare

correct_answer.text: PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the trauma

correct_answers.text: PTSD symptoms usually occur within 6 months of the trauma

questions.explanation:
Symptoms of PTSD usually arise within 6 months of the traumatic event. There is delayed onset in approximately 10% of cases. The essential features of PTSD are autonomic hyperarousal (e.g. exaggerated startle response), re-experiencing of aspects of the traumatic event, and active avoidance of cues that remind the person of the trauma. Anhedonia may also be seen. Insomnia is common. Vulnerability factors for PTSD include low self-esteem/neurotic traits and previous (or family) history of psychiatric problems (especially mood/anxiety disorders).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 402-403.

questions.question_text: What is the severity of his depression?

In ICD-11, ‘mild’ is when none of the symptoms of a depressive episode are intense, and there is some, but not considerable, difficulty in continuing normal activities, and no delusions or hallucinations. ‘Moderate’ is when several symptoms of a depressive episode are present to a marked degree or a large number of depressive symptoms of lesser severity are present overall and there is considerable difficulty in continuing with normal activities, but the individual is still able to function in at least some areas. ‘Severe’ is when many or most symptoms of a depressive episode are present to a marked degree or a smaller number of symptoms are present and manifest to an intense degree and the individual is unable to function, expect to a very limited degree.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnosis best suits his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Substance-induced psychotic illness is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. This has been called alcoholic hallucinosis, but in ICD-11 it is designated as ‘alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations’. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings), and with continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. Unlike delirium tremens, these patients have a clear sensorium. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking; in 5%, symptoms persist with abstinence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with respect to narcissistic personality disorder?

questions.explanation:
Narcissistic personality disorder is not included in ICD-10 or ICD-11, but is included in the DSM-5 Cluster B group. The diagnosis is rarely made outside North America. People with narcissistic personality disorder have a grandiose sense of self-importance. They may be preoccupied by fantasies of success, power, and brilliance, and believe that it is their right to receive special treatment. A high degree of egocentricity occurs in many of the other personality disorders, and so this trait is not in itself diagnostic. In antisocial personality disorder it is associated with a more malevolent feeling towards others, while those with narcissistic personalities are well-disposed, believing that other people admire them.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following symptoms is not classified under Schneiderian first rank symptoms of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
First rank symptoms of schizophrenia are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. First rank symptoms can be categorised as follows:
- Auditory hallucinations (voices heard arguing, thought echo, running commentary)
- Delusions of thought interference (thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting)
- Delusions of control (passivity of affect, passivity of impulse, passivity of volitions, somatic passivity)
- Delusional perception (a primary delusion of any content that is reported by the patient as having arisen, following the experience of a normal perception)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true when comparing ICD-11 and DSM-5?

options.text: Only ICD-11 incorporates dimensional features into its diagnostic and classification system
Only DSM-5 is a classic hierarchical categorical classification system
Only ICD-11 is fundamentally descriptive in nature
Both are based primarily on self-reported symptoms, clinically observed signs, and a few tests
Neither ICD-11 nor DSM-5 allow for multiple comorbidities

correct_answer.text: Both are based primarily on self-reported symptoms, clinically observed signs, and a few tests

correct_answers.text: Both are based primarily on self-reported symptoms, clinically observed signs, and a few tests

questions.explanation:
Both ICD-11 and DSM-5 are fundamentally descriptive in nature and based primarily on self-reported symptoms, clinically observed signs, and a few tests (e.g., of intellectual functioning). A main characteristic of both ICD-11 and DSM-5 is that they are classic hierarchical categorical classification systems. Hierarchical categorical classification systems are exhaustive, their elements are mutually exclusive, and lower levels of the structure are related systematically to specific higher levels. Both ICD-11 and DSM-5 acknowledge the existence of dimensional features that are relevant to mental disorder and incorporate dimensional features into their diagnostic and classification systems. Both ICD-11 and DSM-5 permit multiple comorbidities (i.e., allow a person to meet the criteria for major depression, an anxiety disorder, and a psychotic disorder). Resulting diagnoses may misleadingly suggest that the individual has three disorders rather than a single, complex mental disorder.
Ref: Clark LA et al. Three approaches to understanding and classifying mental disorder: ICD-11, DSM-5, and the National Institute of Mental Health’s Research Domain Criteria (RDoC). Psychological Science in the Public Interest. 2017 Nov;18(2):72-145.

Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 562.

questions.explanation:
Clinical features of mania:
- Elevated mood (out of keeping with circumstances)
- Increased energy which may manifest as overactivity and/or reduced need for sleep
- Formal thought disorder which may manifest as pressured speech, flight of ideas, and/or racing thoughts
- Increased self-esteem, evident as over-optimistic ideation, grandiosity, reduced social inhibitions, over-familiarity, and/or facetiousness
- Reduced attention and increased distractibility
- Tendency to engage in behaviour that may have serious consequences (e.g. preoccupation with extravagant, impractical schemes, spending recklessly, inappropriate sexual encounters)
- Other behavioural manifestation, including excitement, irritability, aggressiveness, and suspiciousness
- Marked disruption of work, usual social activities, and family life
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 320-321.

questions.question_text: What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Dissociative neurological symptom disorder, with paresis or weakness is characterised by a difficulty or inability to intentionally move parts of the body or to coordinate movements that is not consistent with a recognised disease of the nervous system, other mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorder, or other medical condition.
Dissociative disorders are presumed to be "psychogenic" in origin, being associated closely in time with traumatic events, insoluble and intolerable problems, or disturbed relationships. The onset and termination of dissociative states are often reported as being sudden, and the symptoms usually develop in close relationship to psychological stress. The commonest varieties are loss of ability to move the whole of part of a limb or limbs. Paralysis may be partial, with movements being weak or slow, or complete. Various forms and variable degrees of incoordination (ataxia) may be evident, particularly in the legs, resulting in bizarre gait or inability to stand unaided (astasia-abasia).
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

Secondary negative symptoms, which can respond to treatment, occur in association with or result from positive symptoms, affective symptoms, medication side effects, environmental deprivation, or other treatment- or illness-related factors. For example, negative symptoms can be a secondary effect of primary positive symptoms in a patient who becomes socially withdrawn after experiencing delusions of persecution or paranoia, as is the case here.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
De Clerambault syndrome is a form of delusion of love. The patient, usually female, believes that another, higher status individual is in love with them and may make efforts to contact that person. There may be an additional persecutory delusional component where the affected individual comes to believe that individuals are conspiring to keep them apart.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 105.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Acute stress disorder is similar to PTSD with symptoms in the categories of re-experiencing of events (intrusion), avoidance, negative mood, and hyperarousal, but lasting no more than 4 weeks.
Such acute responses are higher in the presence of physical exhaustion, organic factors or disease states. The stressor is usually one that poses a serious threat to security, integrity and social position. The patient may initially be dazed with narrowed attention; disorientation is not uncommon as a result. Sometimes agitation and overactivity are seen. Partial or complete amnesia is not unheard of. Dissociative symptoms seem to predominate in some.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 394.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an ICD-11 diagnostic feature of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation:
ICD-11 characterises frontotemporal dementia (FTD) as a group of primary neurodegenerative disorder primarily affecting the frontal and temporal lobes. Onset is typically insidious with a gradual and worsening course. Several syndromic variants are described that include presentations with predominantly marked personality and behavioural changes or with predominantly language deficits, or with a combination of these deficits. Memory function, psychomotor speed, as well as visuoperceptual and visuospatial abilities often remain relatively intact, particularly during the early stages of the disorder.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

Autism spectrum disorders are a group of lifelong developmental disorders characterised by their effect on social and communication skills, as well as by a restricted, stereotyped, repetitive repertoire of interests and activities. Clinical features include: few or no sustained relationships; odd voice (monotonous and perhaps at an unusual volume, talking at rather than to you); good superficial language but too formal, stilted, or pedantic; impassive appearance with few gestures and abnormal gaze (i.e. limited non-verbal communicative behaviour); focus on rules.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is indicative of disorganised thinking in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Disorganised thinking (formal thought disorder) is a feature of schizophrenia. This may include tangentiality and loose associations, irrelevant speech, and neologisms. When severe, the person’s speech may be so incoherent as to be incomprehensible (‘word salad’).
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed, ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
